ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning.
“I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator.
Recommended Videos
The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason.
Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday night to take a 2-1 lead in their NL Division Series.
Yamamoto dominated his much-anticipated matchup with Atlanta ace Chris Sale, who allowed three runs and seven hits in five innings. Last year's World Series MVP permitted only four hits and one walk while improving to 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason outings, including 10 starts.
His 10 strikeouts were a postseason high for him.
“I was confident and able to control all my pitches today,” Yamamoto said.
The Dodgers can clinch the best-of-five series and take another step toward becoming the first National League team to win three consecutive World Series by beating the Braves again Wednesday night in Game 4.
Atlanta hoped giving Sale extra rest would be a winning formula in the pivotal third game. Instead, after stranding six runners in the first three innings, he gave up the two-run homer to Hernández and a solo shot to former Braves star Freddie Freeman in the fourth.
“He was still touching 100 (mph),” manager Walt Weiss said of Sale. “The stuff was fine. Like I said, maybe the command not perfect. It wasn’t bad. But they did a nice job against him.”
That was all the offensive support Yamamoto and relievers Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz would need.
Ozzie Albies opened the Atlanta ninth with a double off the right-center wall against Díaz and moved to third on Michael Harris II's groundout. Díaz stranded the runner and earned a save when Mauricio Dubón fouled out to right field and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to shortstop Mookie Betts.
A homer for the boo birds
Freeman said he didn't mind being booed by Atlanta fans in the sellout crowd of 42,420.
“I’ve got a gray uniform on,” Freeman said. “I expect boos. It’s OK. ... It’s all love. I still love everybody here and I’m looking forward to tomorrow.”
Dubón made a leaping catch over the left-field wall to rob Freeman of a home run in the third. Freeman wouldn't be denied an inning later. Hernández's homer to left drove in Andy Pages, who singled. One out later, Freeman pulled his 18th career postseason homer to right field for a 3-0 lead.
Lineup change
Roberts moved designated hitter Shohei Ohtani down to No. 5 in the lineup because Ohtani was 3 for 15 in his career against Sale. Ohtani went 0 for 4 with two strikeouts against Sale when the Dodgers lost 1-0 on Aug. 26 in Atlanta.
Roberts correctly predicted Ohtani would have opportunities with runners on base hitting lower in the order.
With runners on first and second in the first, Sale struck out Ohtani to end the inning. With two runners on base in the third, Ohtani reached on catcher's interference by Drake Baldwin to load the bases before Miguel Rojas ended the inning with a flyball to right field. Ohtani walked to lead off the eighth against Brent Suter, Atlanta's fourth pitcher.
Baldwin's bases-loaded grounder to first base drove in Dubón, who singled, in the fifth for Atlanta's only run.
Injury report
Rojas left during an at-bat in the eighth. The second baseman appeared to injure his back on a swing and was replaced by Tommy Edman. The Dodgers announced the injury as lower back pain.
Roberts said Rojas probably won't start on Wednesday and his availability off the bench will be determined before the game.
“I give him credit for conceding that at-bat,” Roberts said.
Weiss made a late change, moving Ronald Acuña Jr. from right field to designated hitter. Weiss said Acuña jammed his knee on a slide in Game 2. Acuña remained in the game but the knee was sore on Tuesday, leading to the lineup change.
Milestone win for Roberts
Roberts now has 71 career postseason wins, tying Tony La Russa for second-most in major league history. Joe Torre is first with 84.
Up next
Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle is expected to face Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow in Game 4 on Wednesday night. Mahle said Tuesday an abdominal pull is now a “non-issue.” He felt the pull before allowing one run in seven innings of a 4-3 loss to Philadelphia in 10 innings during the NL Wild Card Series last week.

Después de que Sale consiguiera cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en el Juego 3 de la SDLN contra los Dodgers, Dubón registró el primer out defensivo y lo hizo de manera espectacular.
Con un corredor en primera y nadie fuera en la parte alta del tercer inning, la exsuperestrella de los Bravos Freddie Freeman conectó un batazo profundo hacia el jardín izquierdo que salió de su bate a 101.3 mph. Dubón siguió la trayectoria de la pelota hasta la pared y calculó perfectamente su salto para realizar la atrapada justo frente a un grupo de relevistas de los Dodgers, quienes se preparaban para que la bola cayera en el bullpen de los visitantes.
La atrapada de Dubón probablemente le robó un posible jonrón de dos carreras a Freeman, pero como mínimo evitó un extrabase y, casi con toda seguridad, una carrera o dos en el episodio.
Los Dodgers llenaron las bases gracias a un sencillo de Will Smith con dos outs y a que Shohei Ohtani llegó a salvo por interferencia del receptor, pero Sale salió ileso al hacer que Miguel Rojas conectara una línea al jardín derecho para terminar la entrada.
Antes de siquiera necesitar la ayuda de su defensa, Sale se unió a Mike Hampton (Juego 2 de la SDLN del 2003) como los únicos lanzadores de los Bravos en conseguir cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en un juego de postemporada.
Freeman se desquitó en su siguiente turno al bate, cuando disparó con autoridad un cuadrangular hacia el jardín derecho-central, el 18vo vuelacercas de su carrera en postemporada, para darle a los Dodgers una ventaja de 3-0.

ATLANTA — The Dodgers went into Game 3 of the National League Division Series knowing they couldn’t be so reliant on the home run, especially with Braves ace Chris Sale on the mound. And yet, in a 3-1 win, it was the home run ball, paired with a masterful performance on the mound from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, that secured the victory.
The Dodgers pulled ahead to a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five series.
The Dodgers tried to score in other ways, putting on six baserunners in the first three innings of the game. But it didn’t work.
They failed to take advantage of some luck and poor defense from the Braves in the first inning, as Mookie Betts beat out a soft ground ball up the first base line and Teoscar Hernández reached on a fielding error by Braves shortstop Ha-Seong Kim.
Yoshinobu gives up four hits and strikes out 10 and Kiké Hernández hits a two-run home run to power the Dodgers to victory in Game 3 of the NLDS.
The lineup shuffling manager Dave Roberts did against Sale had superstar Shohei Ohtani, batting fifth, walking up to the plate with two outs and runners on first and second. His over-anxious approach at the plate so far this postseason followed him into the at-bat. And he struck out whiffing on a slider in the opposite batter’s box.
The next inning, Kyle Tucker hit a two-out single into left, baited Sale into picking over to first base twice, and then stole second. But he was stranded there, as Kiké Hernández went down swinging. All six of the Dodgers’ outs in the first two innings came via the strikeout.
In the third, the Dodgers loaded the bases. Mookie Betts started the effort with a double through the left side of the infield. And it looked for a moment as if Freddie Freeman had capitalized on the opportunity with a runner in scoring position.
He stayed back on a fastball and crushed it to deep left field, on a trajectory to just clear the short fence. But Braves left fielder Mauricio Dubón made a leaping catch, holding into the ball as he slammed into the wall.
Undeterred, the Dodgers kept putting runners on base. With two outs, Will Smith stayed through a slider to single. Ohtani clipped Braves catcher Drake Baldwin’s mitt and was awarded first base for catcher’s interference. Then Miguel Rojas, who’d exit the game in the eighth inning mid-at-bat with what the Dodgers called low back pain, hit a line drive that found leather to end the inning.
So, back to the long ball.
Perennial postseason hero Kiké Hernández delivered the first blow. With Andy Pages on first, after his first hit of the series, Hernández launched a changeup into the left-field stands. Then, two batters later, Freeman turned on an inside sinker and sent it over the right-field fence — where Dubón had no chance to track it down.
Game 3 was billed as a matchup between aces: Sale, whom the Braves tabbed for Tuesday because of his workload in their wild-card series, and Yamamoto, whom the Dodgers partially held back for the first two games with the NLCS in mind.
Yamamoto held up his end of the bargain, limiting the Braves to four hits and one run in seven innings.
He retired 10 of the first 11 batters he faced. The only baserunner in that time, Michael Harris II, bunted for a single. Yamamoto crashed hard, slipping on the slick grass as he tried to pivot but still managing to make a throw to first from the ground.
Shohei Ohtani is batting fifth in the lineup against Braves ace Chris Sale in Game 3 of the NLDS. He hasn’t hit fifth or lower in a starting lineup since 2020 with the Angels.
He only wavered in the fifth, loading the bases with a pair of singles and a four-pitch walk. The Braves’ batting order turned over, and Yamamoto got Baldwin to ground out to first, but that allowed a run. Then he induced Ronald Acuña Jr. to ground out to second to escape the jam. Rojas ranged to his left to field the ball and made an on-target throw even as he slipped on the grass in shallow right field.
Yamamoto didn’t allow another baserunner.
Left-handed reliever Tanner Scott served as the Dodgers’ setup man, throwing a hitless eighth. And right-hander Edwin Díaz came in for his first save opportunity since Aug. 14 against the Brewers.
He gave up a double off the wall to Ozzie Albies to open the inning but retired the next three batters.

During the eighth inning of Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday, Dodgers middle infielder Miguel Rojas exited the game.
Rojas was seen in visible discomfort after fouling off a fastball from Braves reliever Brent Suter.
Rojas started limping back toward the batter’s box and was immediately evaluated by a member of the Dodgers’ training staff and manager Dave Roberts.
Shortly after the injury, the Dodgers announced that Rojas was removed from the game due to lower back pain.
Tommy Edman replaced Rojas at second base.
Rojas went 0-for-3 before departing Tuesday. He has one hit in the series — a double in Saturday’s 5-3 victory.
Rojas is expected to retire after the season is over.
Rojas was a World Series hero last year after hitting a game-tying home run in Game 7 against the Blue Jays, sending the game to extra innings.
The Dodgers went on to win the game in the 11th when Will Smith hit a go-ahead home run.
In Tuesday’s game, the Dodgers’ offense popped off in the fourth inning, when Kiké Hernández and Freddie Freeman homered to give LA a 3-0 lead.
The Braves scored in the fifth when Drake Baldwin grounded out to first after Dodgers starting pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto loaded the bases.
Yamamoto finished with a career-high 10 strikeouts. He tossed 98 pitches in seven innings, giving up four hits, one run and one walk.

Miguel Rojas was the hero for the Los Angeles Dodgers during the 2025 postseason, but his 2026 postseason is off to a much worse start.
The Dodgers infielder Rojas had to exit Tuesday’s NLDS Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in the middle of an at-bat. During the eighth inning at Truist Park in Atlanta, Ga., Rojas fouled off a 1-0 pitch from Braves reliever Brent Suter and immediately came up grimacing.
Rojas was unable to finish his plate appearance and went on to walk off the field with trainers. Here is the video of Rojas’ injury.
Miguel Rojas exits the game after he appears to have injured his back on a swing https://t.co/Rmc25l0OkW
— Talkin’ Baseball (@TalkinBaseball_) October 7, 2026
Dodgers teammate Tommy Edman replaced Rojas in the game, finishing out his at-bat and also taking Rojas’ place in the field. The Dodgers soon officially announced that Rojas had left the contest due to “low back pain.”
Now 37 years old, Rojas is a two-time Dodgers champion who is very beloved by the team’s fanbase. Most notably, Rojas was directly responsible for the Dodgers’ 2025 championship by famously hitting a game-tying ninth-inning home run in Game 7 of the World Series against the Toronto Blue Jays.
But Rojas is now only on a one-year deal with the Dodgers and previously announced that he intends for the 2026 season to be his last. As such, it remains to be seen if that was Rojas’ last-ever at-bat in Major League Baseball.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have had plenty of postseason heroes during their World Series runs in 2024 and 2025.
Last year, the biggest may have been backup infielder Miguel Rojas, who hit a game-tying home run in Game 7 against the Toronto Blue Jays in the ninth inning.
As a result, Rojas has continued to get opportunities in 2026 and was inserted into the starting lineup for Game 3 against the Atlanta Braves in this year's NLDS. He also started Game 2 in place of Max Muncy at third base.

Mandatory Credit: Brett Davis-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect (Reuters)
Rojas was put in to hit against Braves left-hander Chris Sale given his platoon advantage as a right-handed hitter. It did not work out through his first three at-bats as he went 0-for-3 with a strikeout.
Rojas remained in the game for a fourth at-bat in the eighth inning against Braves reliever Brent Suter, who is also a southpaw.
Unfortunately, he did not finish the at-bat. After fouling off the second pitch he immediately reached for his lower back with his left arm.
A trainer came out to visit Rojas and after a brief discussion he was removed from the game with Tommy Edman taking over mid at-bat. Edman popped up shortly after. The Dodgers released an update shortly after. "Miguel Rojas left tonight's game with low back pain," the team wrote on X.
Latest Update on Miguel Rojas
During the broadcast, Ken Rosenthal of The Athletic reported that Rojas originally suffered the setback while fielding a ground ball back in the 5th inning.
If Rojas' injury is serious enough to keep him out for the remainder of the NLDS, the Dodgers would have to replace him on the roster.
That would also keep him out of the NLCS should Los Angeles advance, which would be a huge loss given the postseason experience he brings.

Los Angeles Dodgers infielder Miguel Rojas has exited Game 3 of the National League Division Series in the top of the eighth inning with an injury.
Rojas appeared to tweak his lower back on a swing and is now out of the game. He initially tweaked his back on a defensive play earlier in the game.
He was replaced by Tommy Edman, who popped out on the first pitch he saw.
Rojas drew the start with the left-handed Chris Sale on the mound. It was his second consecutive start after he got the nod in Game 2 with the lefty Ray Kerr starting.
After going 1-for-1 against Kerr before being replaced by Max Muncy, Rojas was 0-for-3 on Tuesday.
What is Miguel Rojas' Injury?
The Dodgers announced Rojas exited the game with low back pain.
Is Miguel Rojas Retiring After This Season?
Rojas is in the midst of what's expected to be his final season in Major League Baseball. The 37-year-old entered the year saying this would be his last. However, he then left the door open for a potential return in 2027 if the Dodgers won the World Series this year.
Before Tuesday's game, Rojas spoke to reporters and still didn't have a firm answer.
"I'm not thinking about that at all. I'm not thinking about my future or anything," Rojas said. "In regards to my retirement or stepping away from the game, I will never think about stepping away from the game because of my performance or my way to play my game. I think there's other things in life that I'm contemplating about that decision. But if I have to tell you right now, I'm not 100% like [Clayton] Kershaw was last year or others in the past that knew for sure they want to go after this year.
"For me it's more, I would say it's a 40/60 right now that I want to stay in the game and I want to play. But it's not about me. It's about the organization. It's about doing what we're supposed to do to help the team win this year. And then after that we will have conversations."
Rojas, who hit the game-tying home run in Game 7 of the 2025 World Series against the Toronto Blue Jays, had a strong season in 2026, appearing in 105 games and hitting .267 with and OPS of .703. He's still an elite defender in the infield.
Off the field, he's a leader in the Dodgers clubhouse.

Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts named potential players who could get a spot in the starting lineup for NLDS Game 3.
The Dodgers' offense hasn't been its best through the first two games of the series, relying exclusively on homers to score all seven of their runs so far. A change of personnel could help the Dodgers string together some hits and bring some more runs across.
Ahead of Tuesday's matchup, Roberts named three players who could insert themselves into the lineup for NLDS Game 3.
"You've got Kiké [Hernandez], you've got [Miguel Rojas], you've got Muncy," Roberts said.
Hernandez provides plenty of positional versatility for the Dodgers, and could stand in at a number of positions if the Dodgers want to approach their matchup against the left-handed Chris Sale with a lineup full of right-handed batters.
The fan favorite's most likely role if he were to start Game 3 would be as the third baseman, keeping left-handed third baseman Max Muncy out of the lineup for a second consecutive game despite hitting homers in each of the first two games of the series, but he could also play either of the corner outfield spots if needed.
Rojas would stand in at second base for Tommy Edman in the most likely case, as Roberts isn't quite ready to move Edman into center to replace Andy Pages despite his rough postseason record.
Who Won't Start for the Dodgers on Tuesday?
In addition to those three players, Roberts revealed Josue De Paula won't have a starting spot against Sale.
"Josue De Paula I don't see being an option," Roberts said.
As a left-handed batter, De Paula's omission from the lineup makes plenty of sense, and he will be available off of the bench for the remainder of the game.
Other than De Paula, Hyeseong Kim and Hunter Feduccia almost certainly won't start, but the rest of the lineup could change as the Dodgers look to find a spark in their offense. With the series tied at one game apiece, the Dodgers need to claim victory in one of their two games in Atlanta to ensure they return home for a game if necessary.
Game 3 could swing momentum in the Dodgers' direction, and they'll do anything to take the lead in the NLDS. Tuesday's game begins at 3:00 p.m. PT.

ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta.
The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2.
With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly.
Díaz Could Close
“I think that we’ve built him up, regained the confidence in him and himself,” Roberts said of Díaz. “I think that it’s certainly a viable option for tomorrow night. I feel very confident with him finishing a game.”
Roberts said Díaz’s most recent outing was about as good as he has seen from him.
“That last outing was as good as we’ve seen him throw, and it’s hard to imagine throwing any better,” Roberts said. “He’s put himself in a position to be the closer.
“In October, I don’t pay too much attention to the long sample of a season in a lot of cases, because in October things happen quickly and you’ve got to be willing to read and react.”
Roberts also praised the way Díaz handled a difficult season.
“Character,” he said. “That’s the main thing. When things aren’t going the best and how players respond, that’s telling.
“The way he stayed the course, dealt with the injuries, went to OKC on a longer rehab to work things out and then took on whatever role we had for him says a lot about him.”
Lineup Changes Are on the Table
Roberts also acknowledged that the Dodgers could look different against Sale.
“I am considering it,” he said. “I think that’s a very fair question. I have to be mindful of it being two games, and then within those two games, what have I seen? Are we seeing good at-bats?”
He pointed to Will Smith as someone whose results have not matched the quality of his plate appearances.
“I think Will Smith is taking good at-bats, just missing some pitches, taking good swings, not chasing much,” Roberts said. “Versus other people maybe expanding, trying to do too much.
“Those are things that you’re trying to make bets on. Then you’re looking at tomorrow with Sale, the history, recency, how guys are prepared and will prepare for Sale. So yeah, I’m thinking through that, and there are possible changes.”
Roberts listed Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas and Max Muncy among the options he could work into the lineup.
“At the end of the day, our guys are our guys,” he said. “I can tweak a lineup. I can insert, take out a player or two, but we still have to go out there and play, execute and take good at-bats.”
Moving Ohtani Is Possible
Roberts said he would consider moving Ohtani further down in the order if he believes it helps the team.
“I would,” he said. “I think moving him from one to two, but going further than that, I’m open to it.
“If I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on. I know that undoubtedly.”
Roberts thinks some of Ohtani’s recent issues have come from trying to do too much.
“I think there’s a little bit of trying to do too much,” he said. “Everything orbits around Shohei in the sense of his talent, and the Braves are going to enter with caution. They’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them.
“Until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to use that playbook.”
He also said Ohtani may be pressing for power.
“Hitting homers, slugging is so much a part of his hallmark in the batter’s box,” Roberts said. “He’s very in tune with what’s being said, what he hasn’t done.
“But that base hit the other way yesterday, that’s production. Against a guy like Chris Sale, that gives you a chance. Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan given the starter.”
Roberts Still Believes in Pages
Andy Pages has also struggled, but Roberts said he plans to keep giving him chances.
“I’m going to continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re going to need him to be an active part of our team.
“This is, for me, given how he has come into the postseason, too small of a sample. He has taken two walks. Tomorrow is not going to be the end-all, be-all because Sale is a tough matchup, but I still want to see good at-bats.”
Roberts believes the main issue is pressing.
“I think there’s trying to do too much,” he said. “When he came back, he was swinging the bat really well, had success, and now I think there’s a little bit of trying too much.”
Freeman Looks Healthier
One hitter Roberts feels especially good about is Freddie Freeman.
“I think he’s gotten into his legs a lot more,” Roberts said. “He’s moving balls in the hitting zone forward. He’s as healthy as he’s been in quite some time. I think the mechanics are sound.”
Roberts credited the five-day break with helping Freeman get his knee into better shape.
“The week off was really crucial for him,” he said. “Being able to manage that with the five days off got him back to health to be able to work through some things without having to perform in a game setting.”
Sale vs. Yamamoto
Roberts expects Sale to attack the Dodgers much the same way he did when Atlanta faced them in August.
“The fastball just sort of bullied us at the top of the zone,” Roberts said. “There was some chase down below, and with the lefties, throwing more two-seamers to keep us honest in and then expand away.”
Still, Roberts believes the Dodgers are in a better offensive place than they were then.
“I do think we are in a different spot,” he said. “The stakes are certainly higher. There is familiarity on both sides. I think we’ll see better at-bats.
“Chris is going to be tough regardless. We know that. We know we’re going to be in for a dogfight, but I just don’t see him bullying us like he did his last start.”
And Roberts feels good about the pitcher the Dodgers will send out against him.
“There should be a lot of talk about Chris Sale, but our guy’s pretty dang good,” Roberts said. “He’s been a very good pitcher in the postseason, so we feel very good about that.
“I think both pitchers are going to pitch well. It’s kind of who grinds out at-bats best.”

As Miguel Rojas is entering the final chapter of a 13-year career, he has a lot to be proud of.
One thing that he is certainly proud of happened over the Dodgers’ bye week last week, when he revealed he flew out to Miami to take his citizenship test and passed.
“As soon as I made the decision that I wanted to do this, I wanted to do it for my family, for my kids and for the future of them,” Rojas said. “So I’m really proud of being an American.”
Rojas, 37, first came to America after he arrived as a 16-year-old prospect out of Venezuela with the Cincinnati Reds.
Since then, he’s developed a whole life in the United States, and he and his wife, Marianna Rojas Gamboa have two children that were born here when he was playing with the Miami Marlins.
“I’m proud of being working here for over 20 years now,” Rojas said. “I’ve been playing professional baseball now for a long time, and that gave me the opportunity to learn the culture, the country, and I don’t take that for granted.”
On the baseball field, Rojas has had a lot to celebrate as he is a two-time World Series champion with the Dodgers.
For Rojas, Dodgers fans will always remember him as a World Series hero last year, when he had a game-tying home run in the ninth inning against Toronto Blue Jays closer Jeff Hoffman to even the score at four apiece.
The Dodgers would get the win after Will Smith made World Series history by hitting the first Game 7 extra-innings go-ahead home run.
While the Dodgers are preparing to play Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday against the Atlanta Braves, Rojas’ time on the baseball field will soon be coming to an end, as he announced at the beginning of the season that he plans to retire after the season.
In his 13-year career in the MLB, Rojas has played five seasons with the Dodgers and has a career 19.6 WAR, a .260 batting average, 61 home runs and 386 RBIs.

The difficult lefty matchup also has manager Dave Roberts considering some lineup changes.
“I think so," Roberts said. "I am considering it. I think that’s a very fair question. I think that I have to be mindful of — it’s two games, and then with the two games, what have I seen?”
Roberts mentioned Enrique Hernandez and Miguel Rojas as potential options to be in the lineup. The only Dodgers with any semblance of success against Sale in their careers are Mookie Betts (7-for-18) and Freddie Freeman (5-for-16).
The Dodgers have been especially reliant on the home run this series, with all seven of their runs coming via the long ball.
In Sunday's Game 2, they went 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position.
Sale faced the Dodgers on Aug. 27, firing a complete-game shutout with 11 strikeouts and just five hits allowed.
Dave Roberts Considering Moving Shohei Ohtani Down in the Lineup

However, he wouldn't commit to anything on Monday.

For what it's worth, Ohtani is 3-for-15 against Sale in his career with five strikeouts.

Move Shohei Ohtani down in the Dodgers’ lineup? Dave Roberts is ‘open’ to it
- Click here to listen to this article
ATLANTA — As the Dodgers mull potential lineup changes for Game 3 of the National League Division Series, manager Dave Roberts said he is “open” to moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the batting order.
In his three seasons with the Dodgers, Ohtani has batted first or second in every game he has started. However, as he has admitted he is trying to “manage” in the aftermath of knee and arm injuries, and as Roberts has acknowledged Ohtani is “not 100%,” the lack of success could compel the manager to replace him at the top of the lineup with a more productive hitter at some point.
“I would,” Roberts said Monday. “I would. I think it’s something that, you know, I think moving him from 1 to 2 — but going further than that? I’m open to it.
“And it’s something that if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team, he’s all-in on. So I know that undoubtedly.”
It would be strange for the Dodgers to bench Shohei Ohtani, but it’s clear that pretending he’s healthy enough to provide meaningful at-bats isn’t helping.
The Dodgers are batting .215 through the first two games of the NLDS, with the Atlanta Braves scheduled to pitch left-handed ace Chris Sale in Game 3 on Tuesday. If the Dodgers lose, they would need to win back-to-back elimination games to advance beyond this series.
Roberts said the lineup changes he would consider include starting Kiké Hernández and Miguel Rojas, both of whom hit well against left-handers. That could mean infielders Max Muncy (0 for 7 against Sale, with five strikeouts) and Tommy Edman (0 for 11 against Sale) might not start.
Center fielder Andy Pages, who batted so poorly last October he was benched for the final three games of the World Series, is hitless in seven at-bats in this series, with four strikeouts.
“I’m gonna continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.
Roberts said he did not envision benching catcher Will Smith, who is 0 for 8 in the series. The Dodgers’ backup catcher, Hunter Feduccia, is a career .205 hitter with no postseason experience.
But, even with the Dodgers’ star-studded lineup, the spotlight shines brightest on Ohtani.
Ohtani has not homered since Aug. 18. He hit .157 between then and the end of the regular season, striking out in 41% of his at-bats. In this series, he has two hits and two strikeouts in eight at-bats, and his inability to refrain from swinging at pitches outside the strike zone has become a glaring weakness.
“He’s not 100%,” Roberts said. “But, at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone.”
Ohtani hasn’t given the Braves a reason to challenge him within the strike zone.
“Everything orbits around Shohei, in the sense of his talent,” Roberts said. “And the Braves are going to enter with caution. And, so, knowing that, they’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them. So until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to kind of use that playbook.”

ATLANTA –– The Dodgers don’t want to overreact to a two-game sample size.
But, with elimination all of a sudden just two games away, they don’t want to wait too long to make changes either.
That’s what dynamic manager Dave Roberts was grappling with on Monday, as the Dodgers gathered at Truist Park in Atlanta ahead of Game 3 of their National League Division Series against the Braves.
A daunting challenge awaits on Tuesday night, when the club will face Braves ace Chris Sale for the first time since he threw a complete-game shutout against them in August.
Thus, even though the team’s quest for a World Series three-peat just began, potential lineup changes were already under consideration.
And even superstar Shohei Ohtani might not be immune.
“I am considering [changes],” Roberts said. “I think that’s a very fair question.”
That didn’t mean Roberts was ready to commit to any significant alterations ahead of a pivotal Game 3, with the best-of-five series tied one game apiece.
He noted the danger of reading too far into small playoff sample sizes this early in the postseason.
Still, he said there were things he was “thinking through” and “possibly kind of some changes” that could be enacted on Tuesday.
One possibility: Inserting Miguel Rojas and/or Kiké Hernández into lineup, perhaps in place of Max Muncy and/or Tommy Edman, to give the Dodgers extra right-handed bats against a dominant left-hander in Sale.
Another, more notable potential option: Moving Ohtani even further down the order from his current No. 2 spot, after he went just 2-for-8 in the first two games of the NLDS while continuing to battle right arm and left knee injuries.
“[We already moved] him from 1 to 2 –– but going further than that? I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “It’s something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why.”
The explanation, of course, wouldn’t be too complicated.
In Ohtani’s currently diminished physical state, he has simply not been the same presence at the top of the order that the Dodgers have grown accustomed to from the four-time MVP.
“Like we’ve talked about, he’s not 100%,” Roberts said.
But also, “I think there’s a little bit of [him also] trying to do too much,” Roberts added. “I think that’s a piece.”
Indeed, Ohtani has suffered from a futile combination so far in the playoffs, failing to either punish pitches over the plate or keep from chasing out of the strike zone.
“It’s hard to have success when you’re out of the zone,” Roberts said. “So I think that’s the thing, then the question is: How do we get him [attacking pitches back] into it?”
A change of mindset could help, especially against a premium pitcher like Sale (who has held Ohtani to a 3-for-15 mark with five strikeouts and only one double in their career head-to-head matchups).
“Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan, given the starter,” Roberts said.
Instead, Roberts pointed to the opposite-field single Ohtani slapped past a shift for his lone hit in Sunday’s Game 2 loss.
“That at-bat yesterday, the block base hit the other way, that’s something that is production,” Roberts said. “I think that’s something where, against a guy like Chris Sale, it gives you a chance.”
The Dodgers, of course, would love to get more pop from Ohtani, who led the team with eight home runs during last year’s World Series trek. Roberts also knows the slugger “feels the responsibility” to provide such power, which might be contributing to his lack of plate discipline.
Thus, for now, taking the pressure off Ohtani’s shoulders by potentially hitting him lower in the lineup might also prove to be prudent.
“At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team,” Roberts said. “And he’s all in on [that]. I know that undoubtedly.”
While Roberts will contemplate other changes beyond Ohtani’s spot in the order, there were a few ideas he outright struck down Monday night.
The big one: Removing Andy Pages from the batting order despite his 0-for-7 start in the playoffs –– one that has felt reminiscent of his historic struggles last October, and been further marred by a consequential ABS challenge he missed in Game 1.
While Roberts said he feels Pages has been “trying to do too much” –– downplaying any lingering effects from the fractured hand that sidelined the center fielder for most of September –– he also said he wanted to give the 25-year-old slugger more leash.
“I believe in him,” Roberts said. “And I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.”
That was all part of the balance Roberts was trying to strike with his team’s season potentially hanging in the balance. It might still feel early for drastic changes. But one more loss, and the club’s three-peat bid will be on the brink.
“Our guys are our guys,” Roberts said. “Yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day, we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats.”

LOS ANGELES, CA — The Dodgers have hit enough home runs to stay alive in this series. What they have not done yet is build innings.
That was the theme running through the clubhouse after Sunday’s 3-2 loss to Atlanta. Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Miguel Rojas all came back to the same point in slightly different ways. The Dodgers are getting runners on base. They are giving themselves chances. Now they need somebody to come through with the hit that keeps an inning moving.
Freeman put it most plainly.
“We’ve got to find a way to score some runs without hitting a home run,” he said. “I think that’s our biggest thing right now. Get guys on base, get that big hit, and hopefully our pitching keeps doing what they’re doing.”
The Dodgers Are Getting Traffic
The Dodgers had chances throughout Game 2 and could not turn them into runs. Freeman said that is where the frustration lies.
“It’s really hard to do,” he said. “You see what’s being thrown at us on their side and our side. It’s hard to get hits in the big leagues, especially in the playoffs. Stringing hits together is very hard, but we’ve had a couple opportunities. Hopefully we can cash them in on Tuesday.”
Betts saw it much the same way.
“I don’t know what’s going on right now,” he said. “We need to get going offensively. It’s not going to be easy, but we knew that from the beginning.
“We had some moments today, but we didn’t come through, but that’s part of the game. We just have to keep giving ourselves moments, and eventually something will happen.”
Rojas pointed to the same missed chances.
“We just missed the big hit,” he said. “We created a lot of traffic, which is good. I think when you’re playing playoff baseball, you’re not facing any easy arms out there. They have really good stuff.
“We’ve got to continue to see what we can do to put together better at-bats when we have runners in scoring position.”
That is the heart of the issue. The Dodgers have found ways to reach base. They simply have not turned enough of those chances into runs.
Bullpen Games Make It Harder
Freeman also talked about the challenge of facing a different look almost every time through the order.
“Bullpen games are hard,” he said. “It’s hard to win those games. It’s also hard to hit those games. We were able to do good in one of them, and they pitched really well tonight.
“It’s tough because you’re facing a different arm every single time you’re going up there. Different angles, different velocities, different things.”
Rojas gave Atlanta credit as well, especially for the work of Didier Fuentes and Robert Suarez.
“They’re throwing the ball really well,” he said. “They’ve got guys with big arms and they know how to use them. Fuentes was really good, and obviously Suarez coming out of the bullpen in that inning with a couple guys on, he was able to get the out.
“Sometimes you’ve got to tip your cap and move on.”
Betts echoed that.
“They’re a good team,” he said. “They did a pretty good job giving ourselves chances. We just didn’t come through.”
Stick With the Plan
The Dodgers also pushed back on the idea that the answer is to simply start swinging earlier or get more aggressive.
Freeman said each hitter has to stay with what works for him.
“Everyone has their own plan and approach going into each at-bat, and you just try to execute it,” he said. “I don’t think anybody’s going to go in and try and start swinging at every pitch. Usually when you do that, you start swinging at bad pitches.
“Just try to control the strike zone like we have been doing and get that big hit.”
Rojas said the same thing in his own way.
“We’ve got a game plan going into the game,” he said. “I don’t think we need to change anything and come on Tuesday swinging at every first pitch because that’s not how baseball works.
“We’ve just got to trust our plan, trust our discipline at the plate. We’re really good at that. I’m looking forward to getting better results.”
That might be the most important part of the whole discussion. The Dodgers know what they are trying to do. They also know forcing the issue can make things worse.
Freeman Feeling Good
One encouraging sign has been Freeman himself.
“I feel good,” he said. “I’ve had a good work week, and obviously the first couple games have been good. Hopefully I can carry it into the road series.”
His home run Sunday was one of the few big swings the Dodgers produced, and it tied the game at the time.
Still, Freeman came back to the broader problem.
“We just didn’t score enough runs tonight.”
Simple as that.
A Short Series Gets Shorter
Betts also put the moment in perspective as the Dodgers head to Atlanta tied 1-1.
“Nobody expected us to go 11-0,” he said. “We know it’s going to be a tough matchup no matter who’s on the mound.”
Chris Sale will be on the mound next, which raises the degree of difficulty even more.
“It’s the same challenges as today,” Betts said. “Nothing’s going to be easy. Obviously we know Chris Sale, so we’ll see how it goes.”
Rojas said the clubhouse understands what is at stake.
“We are not satisfied, to be honest with you, because we got the opportunity to win two games right here,” he said. “But at the same time, you’ve got to understand that the other team is trying to win too.”
He also stressed the need to keep moving after a missed chance.
“The next at-bat is the one that counts,” Rojas said. “A lot of guys in this clubhouse have been in situations where we’re struggling, and once you have an at-bat that can get you what you need to help the team win, that can change things.”
That is where the Dodgers stand now.
The home runs have kept them in the series. The pitching has kept games close. The chances have been there.
Now they need to start turning those chances into runs.

WASHINGTON -- The Los Angeles Dodgers placed shortstop Mookie Betts on the injured list Sunday with a right oblique strain and recalled Hyeseong Kim from Triple-A Oklahoma City.
Betts left Saturday's 10-5 victory over the Washington Nationals after walking and scoring in the first inning. Manager Dave Roberts said the Dodgers believe Betts was initially injured on a check swing during the at-bat.
While Roberts said he was hesitant to put a timeline on Betts' return, he hopes it would be quicker than a four-to-six-week absence.
"He's actually in better spirits," Roberts said. "He's obviously disappointed, but just the way he feels today, I think he's had some dealings with that before and said it's better than he recalls in past experience, so that was encouraging."
Betts is hitting .179 with two home runs and seven RBIs in Los Angeles' first eight games. The 33-year-old hit .258 with 20 homers and 82 RBIs in 150 games last season.
Kim hit .280 with three home runs and 17 RBIs in 71 games as a rookie last season.
Roberts said Kim and Miguel Rojas will likely split time at shortstop while Betts is out. Rojas replaced Betts in Saturday's game and is batting second Sunday against the Nationals. Roberts said Kim is likely to start two of three games in the Dodgers' series at Toronto that begins Monday.
The Dodgers' lineup figures to have a different look as well. Betts hit in the No. 3 spot every game this season after spending much of last year batting second.
"He's Mookie Betts, so it certainly changes," Roberts said. "But that's the great thing about having depth that a lot of teams don't have. A platoon at short and you feel like you've got good matchups, it's not all bad and it gives other guys opportunities. But it's a blow, for sure."br/]

Last week, Alex Vesia made sure to take in the scene.
A full month of baseball, he and the Dodgers hope, still lies ahead this October. Their game last Thursday was nothing more than a regular-season home finale, with the club set to open its postseason back at Dodger Stadium on Saturday in the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
Still, Vesia couldn’t help but feel sentimental as he traversed the clubhouse that afternoon, and sat out in the bullpen with several longtime teammates that night.
For the last six years, this has been home for the left-handed reliever.
As a pending free agent this offseason, it might not be much longer.
“I sent a text in our family group chat that was like, ‘I potentially could have played my last home game as a Dodger, in the regular season,’” Vesia recounted to the California Post this week. “And it was just like, damn.”
Vesia might not be one of the biggest stars of the Dodgers’ modern-day dynasty. But few players have been more important, or reliable, in their ascent to superteam status.
Since arriving as a little-known trade acquisition in February 2021 (acquired from the Miami Marlins, along with Kyle Hurt, in exchange for Dylan Floro), Vesia has been a stalwart in the Dodgers’ bullpen.
He has made 367 appearances for the club, a whopping 150 more than any other Dodgers pitcher in that span (Evan Phillips is next closest at 232). He has posted a 2.66 ERA and 5.7 wins above replacement, according to Fangraphs (ranking fifth among all left-handed relievers in the majors in that latter category during that period).
It was a rise that required personal reinvention, with the former 17th-round draft pick raising his arm slot and cultivating one of baseball’s most deceptive fastballs with the help of the organization’s highly-touted pitching department.
It was a road full of glorious highs, including two World Series championships, and gut-wrenching lows –– both on the field, like when he was optioned to the minor leagues for part of 2023, but especially off of it, after the unimaginable loss he and his wife experienced last October when their newborn daughter passed away during the Fall Classic.
That ordeal has changed the 30-year-old, in ways he still can’t fully verbalize yet.
“It’s been an extremely hard year,” Vesia said, with a set of pink-accented gloves honoring his late daughter resting in his locker behind him.
It has also altered his perspective during what might be his final ride in Los Angeles, making every little moment something to cherish ahead of an uncertain future.
“I’ve learned, especially over the last year, there’s certain moments in life that you need to stop and take it in,” he explained.
Vesia, of course, would love to be back with the Dodgers next year, and beyond. His consistent production and energetic mound presence have made him something of a fan favorite at this point; so much so, a local artist recently unveiled a mural of him in Burbank.
“I’m very thankful to have spent the last six years here,” he said. “I’ve learned so much about myself and the game, just what it takes to be a champion. That’s really, really, really special.”
Still, this lockout-threatened winter raises even more unknowns than usual.
Thus, even though he noted that “there’s still so much in front of us” this postseason, Vesia has allowed some nostalgia to creep in too.
“Even with Miggy and his sort of goodbye to baseball,” Vesia said, referencing likely-to-retire teammate Miguel Rojas, “some of the stuff that he has said about this team, I also resonate with. Like, it hits me too.”
Entering this October, Vesia’s bonds in the clubhouse and, especially, the bullpen –– a group he was first to nickname “The Dawgs” during their heroic contributions to the team’s 2024 title –– have never felt stronger.
Since the beginning of the season, he has been effusive in describing the ways they have supported him in the wake of last year’s tragedy.
In recent weeks, he has felt the unit’s performance collectively click into place, too, with the Dodgers’ relief corps emerging as a potentially underrated strength in their bid for a World Series three-peat.
“It was just like, guys got out of certain innings where … you could just see them start to trust their stuff,” Vesia said. “It’s definitely exciting. I think our guys in the bullpen are catching strides at the right time.”
Per usual, Vesia has been a key part of that resurgence. He posted a 2.64 ERA with 74 strikeouts in 58 innings on the season. More importantly, he improved his previously faulty command down the stretch, walking just one batter in 11 appearances during September.
Now, he’s hoping it sets up a storybook ending to what has been an emotional campaign –– and potentially his impactful Dodgers career.
“The way I view things are a little bit different. The way I go about my business is a little bit different. The way I’m motivated is a little bit different,” he said, while reflecting back on a traumatic 12 months that have made his connections in the organization all the more meaningful.
“Ultimately, I know the job that I have to do,” he added. “But yeah, my motivation for this month is different.”

Dodgers se lo toman con calma: van por el histórico “three-peat” en la MLB
Los Ángeles busca convertirse en el primer equipo desde los Yankees de 1998-2000 en ganar tres Series Mundiales consecutivas.
PUBLICIDAD
Los Ángeles. Freddie Freeman y Emmet Sheehan bostezaron. El mánager Dave Roberts usó pantalones cortos para la práctica de bateo.
Los Dodgers de Los Ángeles se lo toman con calma mientras se encaminan a una postemporada potencialmente histórica.
Intentan convertirse en el primer equipo desde los Yankees de Nueva York de 1998-2000 en ganar tres Series Mundiales consecutivas. Serían el primer club de la Liga Nacional en lograrlo.
Y dejarían las expectativas altísimas para todos los demás.
“No es algo en lo que realmente estemos enfocados. Cuando hablas de ganar tres seguidas, le estás poniendo esa presión extra que no tiene por qué estar ahí“, comentó el antesalista Max Muncy. ”Ganar una Serie Mundial ya es lo suficientemente difícil”.
Los Dodgers disputaron un juego simulado el jueves, mientras se proyectaba el duelo decisivo de la serie de comodines de la Liga Nacional entre Filadelfia y Atlanta en las pantallas de video del estadio. Los Bravos vencieron a los Filis por 6-2 y jugarán en Los Ángeles el primer duelo de la serie divisional de la Liga Nacional, al mejor en un máximo de cinco encuentros, el sábado, cuando se pronostica que la temperatura alcance los 100 grados Fahrenheit (38 Celsius) para el juego diurno.
“Te enfrentas a un equipo que ya pasó por el fuego y ya vivió la emoción”, comentó Muncy.
Los Dodgers han pasado la semana de descanso recuperándose, mientras alternaban práctica de bateo en vivo y en la jaula con juegos simulados en un estadio mayormente silencioso. Aparte de las canciones de entrada al plato, los únicos sonidos eran el chasquido del bate, los gritos de los jugadores desde las bancas y los jardineros avisando a sus compañeros que ellos se encargarían de un elevado.
Freeman aprovechó el tiempo para concentrarse en ajustar la mecánica de su swing mientras lidiaba una molestia en la rodilla derecha. El plan del primera base de 37 años incluía hacer 400 swings “con la esperanza de quitarme los malos hábitos”, explicó.
En el inicio del juego simulado del jueves, conectó un doble ante Tyler Glasnow.
“De verdad me siento bien físicamente ahora mismo y depende de mí resolver la mecánica del swing”, comentó. ”No tengo dolor en la rodilla en este momento”.
Shohei Ohtani, cuatro veces nombrado el Jugador Más Valioso, ha lidiado durante semanas con molestias persistentes en el bíceps derecho y la rodilla izquierda. La rodilla lo frenó para lanzar y el brazo lo llevó recientemente a la lista de lesionados por primera vez con los Dodgers.
Regresó a tiempo para jugar en cinco partidos al final de la temporada.
Aún está por verse qué versión de Ohtani tendrán los Dodgers en la serie divisional de la Liga Nacional. Sin embargo, Roberts dijo que “se siente muy bien físicamente. Sus swings, en general, están en un gran punto”.
La alineación de jugadores de posición de los Dodgers es la de mayor edad en las Grandes Ligas, encabezada por el infielder venezolano Miguel Rojas, de 37 años, Freeman y Muncy, de 35. Ohtani tiene 32. El relevista Blake Treinen tiene 38, pero se perderá la postemporada tras lesionarse el fin de semana pasado.
“Creo que la experiencia va a ser enorme. Sabemos lo que se necesita”, aseveró Freeman
Al mismo tiempo, advirtió que los Dodgers no deben adelantarse.
“Si en este momento piensas en el panorama general, vas a perder de vista las cosas”.

As the Los Angeles Dodgers await the outcome of the final game between the Philadelphia Philles and Atlanta Braves to see who they will face in the NLDS, the team is busy working on keeping their bats and arms fresh and ready for the road to a three-peat that lies ahead.
As Bill Plunkett of the OC Register notes, the last two championship wins were won mainly on the backs of the pitchers – the bullpen in 2024, and key starters in 2025. Could this finally be the year that the Dodgers win it by having their offense outslug the other teams?
"It would be nice to slug our way to a World Series one of these years," third baseman Max Muncy joked on the eve of another postseason run. "We can't keep letting the pitchers take all the credit, right?"
The offense has looked better in the month of September, and they hope to continue that and have those that weren't hitting join those that are. Plunkett has more thoughts from the players on how they're looking to perform in the playoffs here.
As Bill Shakin of the L.A. Times notes, the last two World Series runs have had signature moments from Freddie Freeman, and ponders if this playoff run will have the same.
"My body feels good," Freeman said. "I think that's the main thing. I feel like it's in a good spot to be able to do the work and hopefully fix my swing and everything that's been going on the last couple months."
Shakin goes on to cover Freeman's lackluster second half, and has more quotes from the man himself here.
As the team moves into its newest playoff era, one player is contemplating the end of his own. Miguel Rojas announced at the beginning of the season that he would be retiring at the end of this season. Now, he's not quite so sure. Maddie Chen of the L.A.Times talks about how Rojas is facing the possible end of his career.
"From this moment on, it will be kind of like a day-to-day thing," he said. "And you might get to know that I'm stepping away from the game in an Instagram post, or from me just saying goodbye on a video. I don't know. I don't know how it's going to be, but at this moment, I'm not 100% [certain]."

The Los Angeles Dodgers get to kick back and watch as eight teams duke it out to move on to their respective League Division Series this week. The Atlanta Braves and Philadelphia Phillies will go head-to-head in the NL Wild Card Series before one of them moves on to try and topple LA.
One would think that this Dodgers team would have everything buttoned up well ahead of the NLDS, but there are still a couple of key questions to be answered.
Projecting the Dodgers' NLDS roster with Josue De Paula called upon
Catchers (2): Will Smith, Hunter Feduccia
For some reason, the Dodgers decided to carry three catchers on their Wild Card and NLDS rosters last year — Smith, Dalton Rushing, and Ben Rortvedt — but adjusted ahead of the NLCS by shedding Rushing, who received just one at-bat in the NLDS but otherwise rode the bench.
Rortvedt didn't get a start or even substitution after Game 2 of the NLDS with Smith slowly coming back from injury at the beginning of the postseason. Feduccia figures to play a similar break-glass-in-case-of-emergency role. As a lefty, he could get a start and then an early pull depending on matchups but, barring disaster, it's mostly going to be Smith's show.
Designated hitters (2): Shohei Ohtani, Josue De Paula
The Dodgers clearly want to find a way to bring De Paula with them in October, even if only as a lingering threat on their bench. They're reportedly not entertaining putting him in the outfield at all, and it's not hard to see why. Even if they're confident they'll be able to fix his defense in time, they can't afford any leakage in the postseason.
Ohtani is still shaking off the cobwebs from his 15-day IL stint. He picked up a few hits with promising exit velocity in his return against the San Diego Padres and later against the San Francisco Giants, but there are still question marks around what version of him we might see this postseason.
Infielders (6): Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts, Tommy Edman, Max Muncy, Miguel Rojas, Kiké Hernández
A notable exclusion here is Hyeseong Kim. Although he's in the running to get a spot on the bench and exclusively come into games to pinch-run or for reassurances on defense, there's still a chance he doesn't make the roster if the Dodgers are set on carrying 13 pitchers. Edman and Hernández, though lacking the same speed as Kim, can still offer the same defensive versatility.
Outfielders (3): Andy Pages, Kyle Tucker, Teoscar Hernández
Pages might've found himself in the same boat as Ohtani, but he announced his return to the Dodgers after a month-long IL stint in a big way, hitting .333 with a 1.180 OPS, two homers, and five RBI against the Padres and Giants. No doubt Dave Roberts and Andrew Friedman breathed a massive sigh of relief.
Alex Call will be the odd man out. He was on all four of LA's playoff rosters last year and received sporadic appearances throughout the month, but that was when Michael Conforto was still on the payroll. Tucker and Hernández have certainly had their ups-and-downs this season, but the Dodgers would never seriously consider leaving them out.
Starters (4): Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Tarik Skubal, Tyler Glasnow
There's not much to say about what's probably the best rotation going into the postseason. Snell and Glasnow have both battled injury this season but came back when the Dodgers needed them most. It might be too much to ask that any of Yamamoto, Snell, or Glasnow replicate their dominance from last year, but they'll certainly try.
Relievers: (9): Tanner Scott, Roki Sasaki, Alex Vesia, Evan Phillips, Brock Stewart, Justin Wrobleski, Edwin Díaz, Kris Bubic, Edgardo Henriquez
Just like 2025, this is where things get dicey. The Dodgers' bullpen isn't quite as banged up or as unreliable as they were last year, but they're not the air-tight, bulletproof coterie that their combined salaries suggest they should be. Henriquez will be coming straight off of the IL to rejoin the team in the NLDS, and Díaz, Sasaki, and Scott are all woefully unpredictable.
There is some thought that the Dodgers might carry eight relievers instead of nine, to free up a spot on the position player side for a guy like Kim. In this scenario, we'll stick with them taking nine. If not, Bubic is the most obvious cut. Last one in, first one out.

SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Sunday’s 5-1 victory over the Giants was particularly meaningful for Miguel Rojas, who may have played the final regular-season game of his career. The veteran shortstop was visibly emotional during the broadcast, but after the Dodgers completed their sweep of San Francisco and reached 100 victories, his attention was already turning toward October.
Speaking with reporters after the game, Rojas emphasized the importance of finishing the regular season strong and maintaining the team’s momentum heading into the postseason.
“Yeah, it feels good. Finishing the season strong is something that we as a team put as a goal, not to take that foot off the gas pedal and play until the last out.
“I think it’s really important for us to continue to get momentum into the postseason, and winning is always contagious, and that’s what we’re looking for.
“We’re looking to win another 11 games for us to make history and do something really cool about our legacies and the city of LA.”
Five Days to Prepare Together
The Dodgers now have five days before Saturday’s NLDS opener, and Rojas believes the time together will provide opportunities that go beyond simply resting and recovering.
For the veteran infielder, some of the most valuable preparation comes from teammates sharing their knowledge and helping one another improve.
“Yeah, I mean, it’s going to be important because there’s so many things that we can actually take advantage of on workout days where you get feedback from your teammates more than anything.
“Not just the coaches or the game itself. You get together with your teammates and kind of swing in the cage with them and get together at the same time on the field and talk about pitches.
“You get to face your own pitchers and tell them about the movement of the pitches and ways that they can attack right-handed hitters, left-handed hitters, whatever it is.”
Rojas expressed confidence in the team’s preparation and its collective commitment to another championship run.
“I feel like we got a pretty good plan. We’re looking forward to spending three or four weeks together to finish the season, and we’re all going to make the sacrifice to be 100% in on this one.”
Bringing October Baseball Home to Los Angeles
With more than four million fans attending Dodgers games during the regular season, Rojas was also asked about the significance of securing home-field advantage for the NLDS.
For him, the opportunity to play more postseason games at Dodger Stadium is as much about rewarding the fans as it is about giving the team a competitive advantage.
“Yeah, they deserve it. It’s not just about us,” Rojas said, reflecting on the importance of giving fans the opportunity to experience the biggest postseason moments at home.
“It feels like we’re all really excited about being at home for more games and hopefully get to win at home.”
And while Sunday may have marked the conclusion of his regular-season career, Rojas was quick to point out that his Dodgers journey isn’t finished quite yet.
“We got some more games to play, so I’m really excited about that.”
For a player who has become such an important part of the Dodgers’ clubhouse, there’s still one more chapter to write. And as Freddie Freeman said after Sunday’s game, the team’s goal is to send Miggy out as a champion.
Eleven more wins.

The Giants lost their fourth straight, seventh of eight and seventh in a row to the rival Dodgers after taking four of five in the series to start the year.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have their sights set on winning a third consecutive World Series, which would make them the first team since the New York Yankees, over a quarter century ago, to achieve that feat.
The Dodgers, who are about to open up a series against the rival San Francisco Guardians on the cusp of the MLB postseason, have welcomed back catcher Dalton Rushing off the injured list, but also had to make a corresponding move to open up room on the roster.
The Los Angeles Dodgers Have Optioned Alex Freeland To The Minors
In a corresponding move, the Dodgers have optioned Alex Freeland to the minors, opening up a spot for Rushing.
“The Dodgers have reinstated catcher Dalton Rushing from the injured list and optioned IF Alex Freeland,” the Dodgers reported on X, formerly known as Twitter.
However, the move wasn’t fully well received by fans.
“All Rushing can do is pinch hit. Which means you burn the guy he hits for, Rushing, and a replacement fielder the next inning. Peak Dave Roberts thinking,” one fan noted.
This fan said, “Meaningless series vs. the Giants and could’ve been testing out De Paula in left field this weekend but Alex Call has compromising photos of Friedman apparently.”
This fan said, “Rushing’s elbow is completely fried and this is the second time they’ve recalled him from the IL. I honestly don’t understand it at all.”
Alex Freeland Has Been Optioned To Triple-A By The Dodgers
Freeland was taken by the Dodgers the third round of the 2022 MLB Draft. He began his professional career with Rancho Cucamonga, hitting .313 in eight games, before spending 2023 with Great Lakes, where he batted .240 with nine home runs and 57 RBI.
Freeland climbed through three levels in 2024, finishing the season with Triple-A Oklahoma City. Across 136 games, he hit .260 with 18 homers, 74 RBI and 31 stolen bases.
He started 2025 with Oklahoma City before receiving his first MLB promotion in late July. Freeland debuted for Los Angeles on July 30, collecting his first hit against Cincinnati, and hit his first major-league homer off Yu Darvish on Aug. 22. He hit .190 with two home runs and six RBI in 29 games with the Dodgers, while posting a .263/.384/.451 line with 16 homers and 82 RBI in 106 Triple-A games.
Freeland made the Dodgers’ 2026 Opening Day roster and began the season splitting time at second base with Miguel Rojas.
Freeland has appeared in 89 games so far this season for the Dodgers, and has four home runs with 21 RBI along with a .234 batting average and a .652 OPS.

Dalton Rushing’s breakout season has not exactly gone to plan for himself or the Los Angeles Dodgers.
The upstart catcher got his first taste of extended play in the wake of Will Smith spending much of the first half of the season on the injured list.
Rushing impressively has clubbed 12 homers in only 250 plate appearances. As his confidence grew, the Dodgers faced the reality that Rushing needed to play multiple times a week — even if that meant mixing in starts at first base along with his duties behind the plate.
Unfortunately for Rushing, his season became derailed on Aug. 3. Reports initially focused around a partially torn UCL in his elbow. However, as Rushing recently told Maddie Lee of the Los Angeles Times, that had been a preexisting injury he had been playing through since 2022.
Instead, it’s actually a flexor strain which has sidelined the catcher. Rushing is hoping that he can still be an impact player for the ballclub with the postseason right around the corner.
He's also hoping to avoid offseason surgery.
“I’m pretty confident I can still avoid surgery after the shot,” Rushing said. “Obviously, when I re-injured it the second time, I was almost 70-30, thinking that I was for sure going to need surgery. But after I got the shot and it ran its course, I feel as close to healthy in my arm as I have in a pretty long time.”
Rushing is projected to be activated at some point this week. With only a few games remaining on the schedule, the Dodgers will determine whether he can be a threat off the bench solely as a hitter.
With Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernandez occupying two of the team’s bench spots on a hypothetical roster, the need for a left-handed bat is there.
At this point, Rushing is likely battling with phenom Josue De Paula for a spot on the roster for the first round. De Paula was fantastic in his brief stint in the big leagues — before being sent down on Wednesday — hitting .323 with a whopping 11 walks to just five strikeouts.
Where Rushing has the obvious edge is in collective experience. He likely won’t be able to catch even in an emergency role, though.
Having said that, as someone that can provide pop from the left side, the Dodgers will have to weigh whether experience wins out over a very young yet gifted rookie with less than 50 at-bats at the major league level.

The Los Angeles Dodgers have already punched their ticket to the postseason and rule the NL West once again, but there's a final frontier that eluded them in 2025. They're cusp on clinching a first-round bye in the National League over the Atlanta Braves; a win for the Dodgers or a loss for the Braves on Thursday would lock it up for LA.
The Dodgers would surely love a few days off between the end of the regular season and the start of the NLDS, given how banged up the roster is right now. Shohei Ohtani, Dalton Rushing, and Blake Snell are just a few of their recently injured players who could use a little more time to prepare.
Miguel Rojas would also love to not have to work on October 1, but not because of an injury. According to Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register, Rojas is scheduled to take his US citizenship test on the same day as a potential Game 3 of the Wild Card series. Rojas is looking to follow in the footsteps of Cincinnati Reds slugger — and fellow Venezuela native — Eugenio Suárez, who passed his citizenship test this season, who passed earlier this month.
The Dodgers would love to have Miguel Rojas for every game of the playoffs
Even if the Dodgers were to fall into the Wild Card, they would host all three of those games at Dodger Stadium, but that could still complicate Rojas' participation in that series. LA could always leave him off the Wild Card roster and bring him back for the NLDS, but he's been on almost every Dodgers postseason roster since he returned to the team in 2023. The only exception was the NLDS in 2024, when he sat with injury.
Rojas has been working in the United States since 2010, when the Reds signed him as an international free agent, but his family still lives in his home country. Earlier this season, he declined a move to the bereavement list after his father passed away in Venezuela, and his wife and children were in Caracas during the devastating earthquakes the country suffered in June.
He's set to retire at the end of the season but has major league coaching and managerial aspirations, so staying in the United States after his playing career makes sense.
Barring disaster, the Dodgers' schedule should be clear to let Rojas take the next step toward US citizenship. Dodgers fans are surely wishing Miggy the best of luck.

LOS ANGELES — Josue De Paula's first trial run in the big leagues has come to an end. For now, at least.
With Shohei Ohtani back in the lineup for the Los Angeles Dodgers on Wednesday, Sept. 23 against the San Diego Padres and manager Dave Roberts wanting to get a look at other players competing for a spot on the postseason roster, Roberts said the choice to option De Paula to Triple-A Oklahoma City was easier than it might've appeared on the surface.
"This was the original thought," Roberts said. "That once Shohei gets back, we were going to send (De Paula) out. We had a runway to give him, which we gave him, and he performed more than admirably."
Even that might be an understatement to how well De Paula played.
In a small sample size of 11 games, the 21-year-old showed a confidence and poise beyond his years in the batter's box, controlling the strike zone like a seasoned vet and drawing 11 walks. And once the hits started falling, De Paula showed how dangerous he can really be, mashing three doubles and a home run (his first MLB hit in Miami) while driving in seven RBIs and posting a 1.081 OPS across 31 at-bats. His last regular season game in LA on Tuesday may have been his best yet as De Paula went 2-for-3 with a walk and his first career triple in a 7-0, series-opening win over the Padres.
He's played so well, in fact, that Roberts is seriously considering him for the postseason roster.
"He's a part of that conversation," Roberts said. "He's earned that."
De Paula's value goes beyond the stat sheet, too. Whether he's flipping the bat and yelling, "I really do this!" to his teammates in the dugout after hitting his first career home run, flexing after driving in a go-ahead run on a double or just nodding his head after not chasing a ball outside the zone, there's a level of swag De Paula brings to Dodger Stadium that not only energizes his older teammates, but also captivates fans in attendance every time "Hypnotize" by The Notorious B.I.G. blares over the loudspeakers when the Brooklyn native walks up to the plate.
Per MLB rules, a player who has been optioned can be eligible to play in the postseason as long as his club did so at least 10 days before a series. Optioning De Paula Wednesday would make him eligible to play in the NLDS, Game 1 of which starts on Saturday, Oct. 3, exactly 10 days from now.
That gives the Dodgers flexibility to evaluate the rest of the players vying for a spot in October with limited at-bats to go around in their remaining five games. Roberts specifically mentioned that he wants to get more reps for Miguel Rojas and Kiké Hernández, but the player that De Paula is most directly competing with is probably Dalton Rushing. He's been on the IL since Sept. 5 with right elbow discomfort but is expected to be activated ahead of the final regular season series in San Francisco this weekend.
Rushing won't catch again this season, so his best shot at making the playoff roster is as a lefty bat off the bench, which is the role De Paula would also have, given that president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman mentioned they currently view De Paula as a DH until his defense develops and he can be the capable corner outfielder they believe he can be one day. The Dodgers are unlikely to carry both De Paula and Rushing in October.
But while Rushing, Rojas and Hernández try to make their case in the last few opportunities, De Paula's already made his impression on Dodgers brass.
"Josue's been awesome," Friedman said. "Injected some real-life energy into our team as we got into September and close out the regular season. He handled himself as well as he could possibly do. ... He's done everything he can to put himself in a position to be in the conversation for us as we make our postseason roster."
"He's just a special hitter," Roberts said. "Hitters don't see the ball that quickly out of hand. It's a gift. Just the ability to (not) chase, I think that lines up in the postseason and no moment's gonna be too big for that kid."
De Paula joins the Comets in the middle of the Triple-A playoffs, but Roberts has basically seen enough from the rookie. The onus now lies on the vets.

The Los Angeles Dodgers are looking to do what no Major League Baseball team has done in the last quarter-century and win three consecutive championships.
Despite all the talent on the roster, each name on the 26-man roster come postseason will have more importance than the next. Even someone like Miguel Rojas — who was hitless for a calendar month heading into the World Series — can come up big in perhaps the biggest moment in the history of the sport.
All of this not only boils down to how the two-time defending champions will perform, but who manager Dave Roberts names on the final rendition of the postseason rosters. As entertaining as the impending decision will be for onlookers of the baseball world, the skipper knows the importance of his roster choice as well as anyone.
Josue De Paula and Dalton Rushing appear to be fighting for the same thing come October, but De Paula is still a raw product and Rushing is still on the injured list with elbow discomfort.
“It’s going to be a good debate,” manager Dave Roberts said on Tuesday.
De Paula, the 21-year-old rookie from Brooklyn, NY, put up undeniable numbers in Double-A this season, leading to the outfielder's promotion before registering a single Triple-A at-bat. In his first 11 games in the big leagues, he's hitting .323/.500/.581 with a 1.081 OPS.
Rushing, on the other hand, has plenty more big league experience than De Paula since his promotion last May. Before his first IL stint, Rushing was hitting .253 with an OPS of .809 this season.
The reason for his stint on the shelf was due to a slight tear in his ulnar collateral ligament. After he returned for just four hitless games, he once again hit the injured list, but this time, MRIs gave reason to believe that the flexor tendon was the real issue, something that could potentially be addressed without surgery and assisted through platelet-rich plasma injections.
For either player, this will be an uphill battle. Roberts admitted that for Rushing specifically, it may be just a steeper incline.
“Hitting off the bench is very difficult and so you're just trying to figure out who gives us the best chance," Roberts said. “To be quite frank, it’s going to be tougher for Dalton given the time that he’s missed, and to kind of think that you have three games to get back in the playoff form, which is tough to do. It’s not a knock on him. He’s been great for us. but it’s still tough given that also you’re talking about the consistency of at-bats recently from Josue.
“We have to have those conversations and make a decision.”
